source.title: Defending LLMs against Jailbreaking Attacks via Backtranslation
source.authors: Yihan Wang; Zhouxing Shi; Andrew Bai; Cho-Jui Hsieh

record.tranche_reason: The study reports how often jailbreak attacks, including optimized adversarial suffixes and fixed prefixes, succeed against safety-aligned chat models. This bears on whether those attack forms bypass refusal, but it does not test the proposed first-token mechanism.
record.gate_note: The study's main intervention is a backtranslation defense. Its comparisons of that defense with other defenses are not rows for these claim versions. Rows below retain attack-outcome results for GCG suffixes and fixed adversarial prefixes; other attack methods in Table 2 are not evidence about the listed suffix/prefix bypass mechanism.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper. Its 'No defense' column in Table 2 still reports how often GCG adversarial suffixes jailbreak safety-aligned chat models (Llama-2-13B-Chat, GPT-3.5-turbo), which bears on V4's suffix component. The attacks are borrowed and run in reduced or transfer settings with a strict judge, so this is a new setting rather than a test aimed at V4. No clean-prompt attack rate is reported as a baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude backtranslation is an effective, efficient defense that outperforms baselines and mostly preserves benign quality. They add that it depends on the model refusing clean harmful requests.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests a response-backtranslation defense against jailbreak attacks; it does not use the original fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type and target model affect attack outcomes; the text specifically notes that Vicuna has relatively weak safety alignment and that the PAIR defense-aware setting is more difficult.

fits_no_version.finding: Checking refusal from only the first 20 tokens of the backtranslated-prompt response keeps DSR near the full-generation level on Vicuna-13B with GCG (96% vs 98%). The authors attribute this to models trained to refuse in the first few tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusals by chat models are detectable from the first ~20 response tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The fixed-prefix attack values are only presented graphically and are not described numerically in the text. The reported attack outcomes rely on a GPT-4 judge; no uncertainty estimates are stated. White-box attacks were not tested against the defense-aware system.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack types in Table 2 (PAIR, AutoDAN, PAP) were not retained because they do not specifically test the suffix/prefix bypass mechanism named in V4. Defense-method comparisons were also excluded because they measure the proposed defense rather than the claim's bypass mechanism.

untested.parts: Response prefilling of a compliant start and decoding changes. It is also not shown that bypass works by getting past the opening tokens.

missing.what: No-defense results for AutoDAN on Llama-2-13B (DSR 40%, so 60% attack success) and GPT-3.5-turbo-0301 (DSR 64%). AutoDAN optimizes the same 'Sure, here is' target-output objective as GCG, so a researcher may count it under V4.
No-defense PAIR results on Llama-2-13B (DSR 64%) and GPT-3.5-turbo (DSR 36%). PAIR prompts often instruct the model to begin its reply with 'Sure, here is'.

record.verdict_notes: This is a mitigation study. The attack numbers are its undefended baselines; no clean-prompt rate is reported, and the judge counts a jailbreak only at rating 10. The GCG settings are weakened (200 steps, transfer for GPT-3.5), so low attack success may reflect attack strength rather than robustness. Vicuna rows are excluded because the authors say Vicuna lacks safety optimization.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and resulting refusal changes.
Fine-tuning on benign data and resulting harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence across response positions.

Tests GCG adversarial suffixes and fixed adversarial prefixes. Does not test compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes, or establish that bypass occurs specifically by getting past opening response tokens.
Localization of safety behaviour in weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives produce shallow safety.
Training safety beyond the first tokens and testing whether it holds up.

relationships.condition: White-box per-example GCG suffix (200 steps) on Llama-2-13B-Chat, GPT-4 judge counting only rating 10
relationships.reason: The suffix bypassed refusal on only 34% of prompts (DSR 66%), not near-universally (r2).
relationships.display_finding: With a GPT-4 judge that accepted only a rating of 10, the 200-step suffix bypassed refusal on 34% of prompts (defense success rate 66%).

relation.reason: The no-defense results measure how often adversarial suffixes successfully bypass safety on aligned models.

tranche.reason: The defense evaluation supplies its own undefended-model suffix-attack rates under specified transfer, optimization-budget and judging settings, bearing on V4 in those settings.

source_check.notes: DSR is the complement of attack success under the rating-10 criterion, not a direct refusal rate. The pack accurately paraphrases the authors’ defense conclusion and its dependence on refusing clean harmful requests.

statements.correction: GPT-3.5-turbo-0613; four concatenated GCG suffixes optimized on Vicuna and Guanacos; no-defense DSR=94%; derived ASR=6%; 50 evaluation prompts; GPT-4 judge requires rating 10 for attack success; V4 verdict=limits_scope.
statements.problem: The study-specific numerical statement is correct, but its challenges classification treats limited success as an absent effect without a clean-prompt baseline.
